conclusion.justification: The report concludes that high-quality, long-term evidence shows saw palmetto is no more effective than placebo at improving BPH symptoms, explicitly rejecting the claim.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
# Do Saw Palmetto Preparations Improve BPH Symptoms Long-Term vs. Placebo?

**Conclusion: No, current high-quality evidence does not support saw palmetto as more effective than placebo for BPH symptoms, even at higher doses over longer treatment periods.**

The most rigorous evidence comes from an updated Cochrane systematic review (MacDonald et al., 2012), which found that saw palmetto (Serenoa repens) monotherapy was **no better than placebo** for improving lower urinary tract symptoms consistent with BPH—even when doses were escalated in trial protocols ([Cochrane review summary](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/224887169_Serenoa_repens_monotherapy_for_benign_prostatic_hyperplasia_BPH_An_updated_Cochrane_systematic_review); [PMC full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3513282/)).

This finding is corroborated by the large-scale, NIH-funded **CAMUS trial**, a multicenter randomized controlled trial that tested saw palmetto at up to three times the standard clinical dose over an 18-month period—a longer-term design specifically intended to test whether higher doses or extended use might yield benefit. The trial confirmed no meaningful symptom improvement, though it did establish the extract's safety profile at these doses ([Journal of Urology/CAMUS trial results](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022534712051816)).

The U.S. National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), a government authority that reviews such evidence, explicitly states that "a large study evaluating high doses of saw palmetto and a Cochrane review found that saw palmetto was not more effective than placebo for treatment of urinary symptoms related to BPH" ([NCCIH](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/providers/digest/spotlight-on-saw-palmetto-science)).

While earlier, smaller studies (including the 1998 JAMA meta-analysis) suggested modest short-term benefits, these were generally lower-quality trials with methodological limitations. The best available longer-term, rigorously designed evidence (Cochrane, CAMUS) does not support a real benefit over placebo.

**Bottom line:** Saw palmetto does not appear to meaningfully improve BPH symptoms compared to placebo when studied in well-designed, longer-duration trials, though it appears safe even at higher doses.
